q: The movement of substances in and out of cells is a very important part of living things.
e: Without this movement, cells and organisms could not live very long.

q: All living cells are surrounded by a thin membrane called the cell membrane or plasma membrane.
e: This membrane separates the internal cellular environment from the external environment.

q: Cell membranes are fully permeable and allow all substances to pass through freely.
e: Cell membranes are semi-permeable, controlling the exchange of specific substances.

q: Substances can only cross the protective cell membrane by diffusion, osmosis, or active transport.
e: These are the primary mechanisms for substance movement across the membrane.

q: The plasma membrane is made up primarily of a bilayer of phospholipids with embedded proteins, carbohydrates, glycolipids, and glycoproteins.
e: This describes the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane.

q: In plant cells, the plasma membrane contains cholesterol.
e: Cholesterol is present in the plasma membrane of animal cells, not plant cells.

q: The membrane is composed of two layers of phospholipid molecules.
e: This forms the fundamental phospholipid bilayer structure.

q: Phospholipids are lipid molecules consisting of a phosphate head, which is attached to the glycerol molecule.
e: Two fatty acid tails are also attached to the same glycerol molecule.

q: The phosphate head of these molecules is in contact with aqueous fluid both inside and outside of the cell, making their surfaces hydrophobic.
e: The phosphate head surfaces are hydrophilic (water-loving), not hydrophobic.

q: The fatty acid tails are facing each other and forming a hydrophobic or non-polar region in the interior of the membrane.
e: This hydrophobic core prevents the free passage of water-soluble substances.

q: Lipid-soluble (non-polar) material can easily slip through the membrane.
e: The hydrophobic interior of the membrane allows non-polar substances to pass readily.

q: The small hydrophobic molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the membrane slowly.
e: Small hydrophobic molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the membrane rapidly.

q: Small polar molecules such as water and ethanol can also pass through the membrane but slowly.
e: Despite being polar, their small size allows them to pass through, albeit at a slower rate.

q: The cell membrane restricts the diffusion of highly charged molecules, such as ions, and large molecules such as sugars and amino acids.
e: These substances require specific transport proteins to cross the membrane.

q: The principal components of the cell membrane are lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates.
e: Each of these components plays a distinct and vital role in membrane function.

q: The phospholipid layer acts as a barrier to most water-soluble substances and prevents tight packing.
e: It provides the basic bilayer for other components to bind to.

q: Cholesterol maintains the fluidity of the membrane and prevents the membrane from becoming rigid.
e: It also stabilizes the hydrophobic layer and strengthens the basic bilayer.

q: Cholesterol prevents ions and hydrophilic molecules from passing through the membrane.
e: This reinforces the barrier function of the phospholipid bilayer.

q: Integral proteins are found on the exterior or interior surfaces of membranes, attached either to integral proteins or to phospholipid molecules.
e: This describes peripheral proteins; integral proteins are embedded in and may span the plasma membrane.

q: Integral proteins may serve as channels or pumps to move materials into or out of the cell.
e: This is a primary function of transmembrane integral proteins.

q: Both integral and peripheral proteins may serve as enzymes, as structural attachments for the fibers of the cytoskeleton, or as part of the cell's recognition sites.
e: Proteins in the membrane are highly diverse in their structure and function.

q: Carbohydrates are found on the interior surface of cells and are bound either to proteins forming glycoproteins or to lipids forming glycolipids.
e: Carbohydrates are found on the exterior surface of cells, not the interior.

q: Carbohydrates provide cushioning and protection for the plasma membrane and are important in cell recognition.
e: They also act as a glue to attach cells together.

q: Substances may pass through the cell membrane either passively by diffusion or actively by some form of active transport.
e: These represent the two main categories of membrane transport based on energy requirement.

q: Passive transport is a movement of ions and other atomic or molecular substances across cell membranes without need of energy input.
e: It relies on the natural kinetic energy of the molecules.

q: The main kinds of passive transport are diffusion, facilitated diffusion, and osmosis.
e: All three processes move substances down their concentration or water potential gradients.

q: Diffusion is the random movement of molecules or ions of substances from an area of low concentration to an area of high concentration.
e: Diffusion is the movement from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration.

q: The natural kinetic energy of the molecules or ions causes the random movement in diffusion.
e: This movement continues until an equilibrium situation is reached.

q: As a result of diffusion, molecules or ions tend to reach an equilibrium situation, where they are evenly spread within a given volume of space.
e: At equilibrium, there is no net movement of molecules, though random motion continues.

q: Glycerol molecules are large and cannot easily slip through the phospholipid bilayer into the cell.
e: Glycerol molecules are small and can easily slip through the phospholipid bilayer.

q: Oxygen gas diffuses into the red blood cells from the alveoli in the lung, while carbon dioxide diffuses the opposite way.
e: This is a classic example of gas exchange via simple diffusion.

q: The greater the difference in concentration, the more rapid the rate of diffusion.
e: A steeper concentration gradient drives a faster rate of diffusion.

q: High temperature decreases the kinetic energy of molecules, thus decreasing the rate of diffusion.
e: High temperature increases the kinetic energy of molecules, thus increasing the rate of diffusion.

q: An increase in surface area increases the rate of diffusion, whereas a thicker membrane reduces the rate of diffusion.
e: These are key physical factors affecting the efficiency of diffusion.

q: As the density of a solvent increases, the rate of diffusion increases.
e: As the density of a solvent increases, the rate of diffusion decreases.

q: Non-polar or lipid-soluble materials pass through the plasma membrane easily and allow a faster rate of diffusion.
e: This is due to their compatibility with the hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer.

q: The greater the distance that a substance must travel, the slower the rate of diffusion.
e: Diffusion is only efficient over very short distances.

q: Facilitated diffusion is a type of active transport that allows substances to cross membranes with the assistance of special transport proteins.
e: Facilitated diffusion is a type of passive transport, not active transport.

q: Molecules and ions such as glucose, sodium ions, and chloride ions are unable to pass through the phospholipid bilayer of cell membranes.
e: They require assistance from specific membrane proteins to cross.

q: These substances can be transported into the cell using ion channel proteins and carrier proteins that are embedded in the cell membrane.
e: These proteins provide a pathway for hydrophilic or large molecules.

q: Ion channel proteins allow specific ions to pass through the protein channel and are regulated by the cell to be either open or closed.
e: This regulation controls the passage of substances into the cell.

q: Carrier proteins bind to specific molecules, change shape, and then deposit the molecules across the membrane, returning to their original shape once transport is completed.
e: This conformational change is the mechanism of carrier-mediated transport.

q: The diffusion of glucose into and out of the red blood cells requires channel proteins because glucose is hydrophobic and soluble in lipids.
e: Glucose requires carrier/channel proteins because it is hydrophilic and insoluble in lipids.

q: Osmosis is defined as the net movement of water from a region of high water potential to a region of low water potential down a water potential gradient through a partially permeable membrane.
e: This is the precise definition of osmosis.

q: The tiny holes in the membrane allow large solute molecules to pass through, but the small water molecules are too big to pass.
e: The tiny holes allow small water molecules to pass through, but the large solute molecules are too big.

q: If a cell is placed in a solution of lower water potential, water leaves the cell by osmosis.
e: Water moves out of the cell to equilibrate the water potential gradient.

q: Water potential is a measure of the ability of water to move out of a solution by osmosis.
e: It is influenced by water availability and pressure exerted on the water.

q: A dilute solution has a low water potential.
e: A dilute solution (containing a lot of water molecules) has a high water potential.

q: A concentrated solution has a low water potential.
e: It contains fewer free water molecules, resulting in a lower water potential.

q: An isotonic solution has an osmotic concentration of solutes that is the same as that in the cell.
e: In an isotonic solution, there is no net movement of water into or out of the cell.

q: A hypotonic solution has an osmotic concentration of solutes that is higher than that in the cytoplasm of the cell.
e: A hypotonic solution has an osmotic concentration that is lower than that in the cytoplasm (higher water potential).

q: A hypertonic solution has an osmotic concentration of solutes that is higher than that in the cytoplasm of the cell.
e: This causes water to leave the cell by osmosis.

q: If water enters a plant cell by osmosis, the cytoplasm will swell and the cell becomes turgid.
e: The plant cell is supported by its cell wall and will maintain its turgidity without bursting.

q: If water leaves a plant cell by osmosis, the cytoplasm will shrink, but the cell wall fails to shrink due to its tough structure.
e: The cytoplasm eventually tears away from the cell wall, a process known as plasmolysis.

q: Animal cells have a cell wall and a membrane.
e: Animal cells have no cell wall, just a membrane.

q: As water moves out, animal cells become flaccid and crenated.
e: This shrinking and wrinkling occurs in hypertonic solutions.

q: If water enters an animal cell by osmosis, the animal cell swells and bursts.
e: Without a cell wall, animal cells cannot withstand the internal pressure of excess water.

q: In mammals, the kidneys play a vital part in the process of osmoregulation.
e: They help keep the blood plasma and body fluid at the same water potential as the cytoplasm.

q: Active transport is the transport of substances from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
e: Active transport is the transport of substances from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration.

q: Active transport occurs against the concentration gradient with the use of the cell's energy (ATP).
e: This distinguishes it from passive transport, which does not require energy.

q: A carrier protein is required in active transport.
e: The substance binds to a receptor site on the carrier protein.

q: A molecule of ATP is required to change the shape of the carrier protein, and the substance is released on the other side of the membrane.
e: The hydrolysis of ATP provides the energy for this conformational change.

q: Active transport takes place only in living, respiring cells.
e: This is because it depends on the continuous production of ATP through respiration.

q: Factors that increase the production of ATP decrease the rate of active transport.
e: Factors that increase the production of ATP increase the rate of active transport.

q: The rate of active transport depends on temperature and oxygen concentration, which affect the rate of respiration and the production of ATP.
e: Cells with more mitochondria can carry out faster rates of transport.

q: Cyanide prevents the synthesis of ATP during cellular respiration, but it does not stop active transport.
e: Cyanide prevents ATP synthesis and therefore stops active transport.

q: If ATP is added artificially, active transport starts again.
e: This demonstrates the direct dependence of active transport on ATP availability.

q: Endocytosis is the uptake of substances by a cell in mass or in bulk forming vesicles.
e: It is a form of active transport that requires energy.

q: Endocytosis can be divided into two types: phagocytosis and pinocytosis.
e: These represent the uptake of solid particles and liquid droplets, respectively.

q: Phagocytosis is cell drinking in which liquid and dissolved substances are taken into the cell.
e: Phagocytosis is cell eating in which solid particles (e.g., bacteria) are taken in.

q: Phagocytosis happens when an amoeba takes in food.
e: White blood cells also use phagocytosis to engulf pathogens.

q: Folds of the plasma membrane extend outward and engulf particles to be ingested and form a vacuole around it.
e: This is the first step in the process of phagocytosis.

q: The vacuole then frees itself from the membrane and the cytoplasm, forming a food vacuole or phagosome.
e: This isolates the ingested material within the cell.

q: Lysosomes fuse with the vacuole or phagosome and release hydrolases into it.
e: These enzymes are responsible for digesting the contents of the vacuole.

q: When the content is digested, the products are absorbed and the vacuole disappears.
e: Any undigested content will be egested through the reverse of the process.

q: Pinocytosis is cell drinking in which liquid and dissolved substances are taken into the cell in the form of vesicles.
e: It is the same process as phagocytosis except that no solid particles are involved.

q: In pinocytosis, tiny droplets of fluid are trapped by cilia and pinched off from the cytoplasm as vesicles.
e: Tiny droplets of fluid are trapped by microvilli, not cilia.

q: In the small intestine, pinocytosis is known as micropinocytosis for the uptake of fat droplets.
e: This occurs in the epithelial cells of the small intestine.

q: Pinocytosis occurs in liver cells, the cells in the proximal convoluted tubule of nephron, and white blood cells.
e: These cells utilize pinocytosis for various absorptive and defensive functions.

q: Exocytosis is the reverse of endocytosis in which the cell egests or secretes substances.
e: It is the mechanism by which cells expel materials.

q: In exocytosis, a vacuole with waste products or a vesicle from the Golgi complex moves towards the plasma membrane, fuses with it, and releases its content.
e: This fusion allows the contents to be expelled to the outside of the cell.

q: Cell egestion happens in glandular cells such as cells in the thyroid glands that secrete hormones.
e: This describes cell secretion; cell egestion happens in amoeba or white blood cells expelling undigested solid.

q: Cell secretion happens in cells in the tubular glands in large intestines that secrete mucus.
e: This is a classic example of exocytosis for cell secretion.
